questions.q: A dagesh is put inside the letter ב. What sound does it now have?
questions.why: With the dot it is the hard sound b, without it the soft sound v. Nothing else in the word gives it away: אָבִיב has no dagesh in either ב, so it is /aviv/, while בַּיִת has one and is /bayit/.

questions.q: Which three letters actually change their sound with a dagesh in Israeli Hebrew?
questions.why: בּ כּ פּ are b, k, p with the dot and v, kh, f without it. ג ד ת take a dagesh too and it makes no audible difference today; the full traditional six are remembered as בְּגַ״ד כְּפַ״ת.

questions.q: On which side does the dot sit when ש is read sh?
questions.why: שִׁין takes its dot on the right, שִׂין on the left. The right is the side a Hebrew word starts from, which is the mnemonic worth keeping; and in unpointed text, where no dot is written at all, assuming sh is right far more often than not.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for the sun, read /shemesh/.
questions.why: Both dots are on the right, so both letters are שִׁין. It is also a segolate: two סֶגּוֹל signs, and the stress at the front.

questions.q: What is the first sound of שִׂמְחָה?
questions.why: The dot is on the left, so this is שִׂין and the word is /simkha/. שִׂין is much rarer than שִׁין, which is why the dot on the left is worth noticing every time you see it.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for a house, read /bayit/.
questions.why: The dagesh in the ב is what makes it b. Take the dot away and the same four letters would read /vayit/, which is nothing at all.
Spring, /aviv/. Neither ב carries a dagesh, so both are v, and the opening א is silent. Two identical letters, one sound, no dots to hear.
A language, and also a lip, /safa/. The dot is on the left, so it opens with s; with the dot on the right it would be /shafa/, which is not a word.
More, still, /od/. The ו here is not the consonant v: the dot above and to its left makes it a חוֹלָם מָלֵא, the vowel o. The opening ע is silent, so the word begins on that vowel.

questions.q: Put the six letters of בְּגַ״ד כְּפַ״ת into their traditional order.
questions.why: ב ג ד כ פ ת, alef-bet order, held together by the nonsense word בְּגַ״ד כְּפַ״ת. All six once had two sounds; three of them still do, and grammar books go on naming the whole set.

questions.q: The final ך of מֶלֶךְ carries no dagesh. How is the word read?
questions.why: Without a dagesh, כ is the throat sound kh, the same as ח. With one it would be k, as in כֶּסֶף. A final letter very often turns up without a dagesh, so the soft sound is the safe guess at the end of a word.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for a commandment, read /mitzva/, in the full spelling this course uses.
questions.why: Two vavs, because the first one is a consonant v. A single ו there would be read as the vowel o or u, so modern full spelling doubles it, exactly as אֲוִויר doubles its own.

questions.q: The ב of סַבָּא has a dagesh, but it would sound like b there anyway. What is the dot doing?
choices: Marking a consonant that was once said twice
Marking the letter as the root's first letter
Nothing; it is a printing habit
questions.why: That is a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, the doubling dagesh, as against the דָּגֵשׁ קַל that switches b, k, p on. Israeli Hebrew does not pronounce doubled consonants, so it is invisible in speech, but it flags a letter that has swallowed another one and that is how verb patterns are spotted later.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the two jobs a dagesh does, with an example of each.
a: דָּגֵשׁ קַל switches a soft sound to a hard one in בּ כּ פּ: בַּיִת is /bayit/ with the dot and would be /vayit/ without it. דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק doubles a consonant that is already hard, as in סַבָּא, where the ב would be b in any case. The first is audible in modern Hebrew, the second is not, but the second still carries information: it marks a letter that has absorbed another and so identifies the pattern a word was built on.
questions.why: The same dot doing two unrelated jobs is the confusing part. Reading aloud, only the first matters; reading for structure, the second is the more useful of the two.
